entities.name: William F. De Saussure
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
William Ford De Saussure (1792–1856) was an American Democratic politician from South Carolina who briefly served in the U.S. Senate (1852) following the death of John C. Calhoun's successor — appointed to fill a vacancy. A South Carolina Democrat and lawyer in the Nullification tradition of his state, De Saussure represented the Deep South's most intense pro-slavery and states' rights political culture during the antebellum period. South Carolina in the early 1850s was the hotbed of secessionist thought — the state that had pioneered Nullification under Calhoun and that was already contemplating secession during the crisis that produced the Compromise of 1850.

His brief Senate service — just months filling a vacancy — prevented him from playing a major role in the major debates.

His family was among South Carolina's most distinguished Huguenot-descended legal families.

He was a Columbia lawyer and planter-politician.
